n001.text: Korea's big three marts: E-Mart, Homeplus, Lotte Mart.

n003.text: but as sales fall, stores are closing.

n004.text: No. 2 Homeplus recently filed for bankruptcy protection.

n005.text: But one chain is doing the opposite: more stores, sales up hundreds of millions a year.

n006.text: It's Costco, the US members-only warehouse club that came to Korea in 1998.

n007.text: In 2024, with just 19 stores in Korea, Costco outsold Lotte Mart and its 100-plus stores, stunning the retail industry.

n008.text: In a year or two, it may pass Homeplus too,

n009.text: and reportedly become Korea's No. 2 big-box chain.

n010.text: Meanwhile, Costco is thriving not just in Korea but in the US, against giants Amazon and Walmart,

n011.text: with its stock up nearly tenfold over the past decade. So how did Costco, a members-only store,

n012.text: win over so many shoppers around the world?

n013.text: In this video, we'll explore Costco's history.

n017.text: Costco's founder, Jim Sinegal. He started it in 1983 and listed it on NASDAQ just two years later,

n018.text: earning the nickname 'the Steve Jobs of retail.' But in an interview, Jim said his retail know-how

n021.text: and then Price Club in 1976. He was Sol Price, known as the father of American retail.

n022.text: Sam Walton, founder of Walmart, the world's largest retailer, also called Sol the father of retail, saying he'd stolen many of Sol's ideas.

n023.text: To understand Costco's history, we first need to know Sol Price.

n024.text: Surprisingly, until he founded FedMart in his late 30s, Sol was a lawyer with no retail background at all.

n025.text: He got into retail after his father-in-law died,

n026.text: and his mother-in-law asked him to manage the estate.

n027.text: Looking to lease the estate's empty 21,000-square-foot San Diego warehouse, Sol

n028.text: heard of a then-hot LA discount store:

n030.text: In Fedco, LA's federal employees pooled their dues

n031.text: to buy goods in bulk and resell them cheaply to members. It was a members-only discount store for federal workers, named for

n033.text: Fedco's prices were so low that even civil servants from San Diego, a five-to-six-hour round trip, drove up to shop. Hearing this, Sol went to see it himself.

n034.text: Arriving in LA, Sol toured Fedco's packed store

n035.text: and pictured Fedco in his father-in-law's warehouse.

n036.text: But Fedco wasn't a for-profit business.

n037.text: It was a co-op built to serve LA's government workers. So Fedco saw no reason to expand to other areas, and flatly turned down Sol's offer to open a store there.

n039.text: but instead of disappointment, he felt something else welling up: this was his big chance.

n040.text: In 1954, in that empty warehouse, Sol copied Fedco: a members-only discount store for civil servants

n041.text: called FedMart, launching his retail career.

n042.text: Since the business was all but guaranteed to succeed from day one,

n043.text: FedMart made $3 million in year one.

n044.text: And unlike Fedco, FedMart was purely for profit,

n046.text: soon becoming a major retailer with dozens of stores across the US Southwest.

n047.text: But FedMart's success ended up shaking the entire US retail industry, quite by accident.

n048.text: Back then, the US had "fair trade" laws that let manufacturers, not retailers, set the prices of the goods stores sold.

n049.text: These laws were meant to stop big chains from buying from manufacturers and selling at a discount to undercut small retailers. But with no discounts allowed and goods always sold at full price,

n050.text: the laws did nothing for consumers.

n051.text: But Sol, a lawyer, had seen a loophole in these laws from the day he founded FedMart.

n052.text: The laws covered "general retailers," and FedMart, a membership store serving only government employees, wasn't one.

n053.text: In other words, FedMart members could buy goods cheaply, free from those laws.

n054.text: As FedMart grew across regions, word spread that it sold cheaply to government workers.

n055.text: Then in 1962, Walmart, Kmart and other discounters arrived and found ways around fair trade laws. Most opened in rural towns and small cities where enforcement was lax.

n056.text: As everyday shoppers began enjoying the savings, fair trade laws slowly lost their teeth.

n057.text: In 1975, unable to hold back the tide, the laws were finally repealed.

n058.text: Meanwhile, Sol, who had unwittingly helped kill a bad law and launch America's discount store boom, sought new investors to grow FedMart.

n059.text: But the partner he chose would once again steer Sol's life off course.

n062.text: a successful German retailer, hoping to grow FedMart further.

n063.text: But after paying a fortune for a stake in FedMart, Hugo did an about-face, seized the board and voted to fire Sol, the company's founder. In fact, Hugo wasn't after FedMart's business.

n064.text: He wanted the real estate under its dozens of stores all along.

n065.text: Sol was 60 when he was fired from the company he'd built over 20 years.

n066.text: He had actually planned to hand FedMart over to Hugo and ease into retirement.

n067.text: But Hugo's betrayal made Sol furious, and at 60, he decided to start a new business all over again.

n068.text: But the discount market was already packed.

n069.text: It was a tough field for any newcomer. That's when Sol came up with a whole new kind of discount store.

n070.text: Not for consumers, but for restaurants,

n071.text: shops, and other small business owners.

n072.text: His store for business owners differed from consumer discount stores in many ways. It was a huge, bare-bones warehouse where goods sat on display in bulk, still in the manufacturer's packaging, much like a wholesale depot.

n073.text: So the warehouse store you find at Costco today was originally Sol's idea.

n074.text: On top of that, Sol brought back FedMart's membership fee model.

n075.text: He believed earning money from membership fees, rather than from sales, was a better way to draw customers.

n076.text: With no markup needed on prices, he could sell goods far cheaper than his competitors.

n077.text: And so, having dreamed up the idea of a membership warehouse store, Sol

n078.text: In July 1976, he opened Price Club, combining his last name with 'club' for a members-only store.

n079.text: But contrary to Sol's hopes, Price Club didn't take off right away.

n080.text: Small business owners weren't used to paying a fee just to shop,

n081.text: and convincing them one by one to try Price Club was a real struggle.

n082.text: That's when Sol had another idea.

n083.text: He dropped the idea of a store just for business owners and partnered with companies and public agencies, so their employees naturally became Price Club members. As more people joined, word spread that you could shop for less,

n084.text: and soon business owners and everyday shoppers alike flocked to join.

n085.text: Meanwhile, as crowds grew, hot dog vendors began popping up outside Price Club stores.

n086.text: Watching shoppers happily munching on hot dogs, Sol decided Price Club should sell its own.

n087.text: The hot dog and soda combo they started selling was priced at just $1.50.

n088.text: Sol explained it wasn't about profit,

n089.text: but a service for members who came to shop at Price Club, he explained.

n090.text: That combo is the origin of the $1.50 hot dog deal Costco still sells today, 40 years later.

n091.text: As Price Club grew, two people became very interested in Sol's membership warehouse business model.

n093.text: Jeff Brotman, a lawyer and entrepreneur.

n094.text: Sam Walton visited Sol in person, saying he wanted to model a Walmart warehouse store on Price Club. Sol gladly agreed and let him explore the stores as much as he liked.

n096.text: Sam began recruiting members for his membership warehouse store, Sam's Club.

n097.text: Jeff Brotman, meanwhile, didn't go to Sol. He tracked down a Price Club executive and pitched starting a membership warehouse business. The man who got that call was Jim Sinegal, who would later found Costco.

n098.text: In 1955, Jim Sinegal, a college student looking for a part-time job, started as a cashier at FedMart, which was hiring.

n099.text: FedMart's unique management style won Jim over. Sol believed employees had to be proud of their workplace to give customers the best value, so

n100.text: FedMart paid the highest wages in the industry and even offered health insurance, rare at the time.

n101.text: Sol, the boss, noticed that even as a part-timer,

n102.text: Jim worked as hard as full-time staff.

n104.text: and when Sol later left FedMart to found Price Club, Jim followed him and became one of its key executives.

n106.text: Jim was a seasoned retail veteran.

n107.text: Then one day, a man named Jeff Brotman pitched Jim a new membership warehouse business. Instead of the Southwest, where Price Club already ruled,

n108.text: He argued they could succeed by targeting a niche in the Northwest, around Seattle.

n109.text: Copying the model of his mentor of 30 years bothered Jim,

n110.text: but Sol, who'd let Sam Walton start Sam's Club,

n111.text: was very relaxed about others copying his business model. So on September 15, 1983, in Seattle, Jim and Jeff

n112.text: they founded Costco, their very own membership warehouse company.

n115.text: Jim took what he'd learned at FedMart and Price Club

n116.text: and applied it to Costco, one step at a time. The first lesson from Sol?

n120.text: and then you can't offer members the lowest prices.

n121.text: Sol taught Jim back at Price Club that if members can't get the lowest prices, they have no reason to buy a membership.

n122.text: So instead of advertising, Costco sold goods cheaper than anyone,

n123.text: letting word of mouth turn shoppers into Costco members.

n124.text: Jim also put gas stations, pharmacies, and optical shops in stores,

n125.text: offering services far cheaper than regular gas stations, pharmacies, and optical shops. This, too, was a tactic Sol had used at FedMart.

n126.text: Costco could charge less than ordinary stores because it never intended to make money from its gas stations, pharmacies, or optical shops.

n132.text: but as a benefit for the loyal members who shop at Costco.

n133.text: One way it differed from Price Club?

n134.text: Costco expanded much, much faster. While Price Club cautiously added stores one by one,

n135.text: Costco opened store #2 a month after the first, and #3 three months later,

n136.text: growing at a breathtaking pace. Price Club, however, after Sol Price retired in 1988,

n137.text: began losing ground, squeezed by the aggressive expansion of Costco and Walmart's Sam's Club.

n140.text: After absorbing Price Club, Costco kept growing. And in 1995 came the private label no Costco story is complete without:

n143.text: Costco's product strategy is pretty unique.

n144.text: While discount stores like Walmart stock over 100,000 different items, Costco carries only 4,000 hand-picked products.

n145.text: That's because Costco believes members don't want endless variety—they want the best price.

n146.text: In the early-to-mid '90s, Jim noticed suppliers raising prices when raw material costs rose, but never lowering them when costs fell. He took bold action.

n147.text: His solution: Costco would make its own private-label, or store-brand, products and sell them for less than the suppliers' goods. But at first, each kind of product carried its own brand name.

n149.text: As random brand names piled up,

n150.text: Jim started thinking of one name to unite them all.

n151.text: Then, thanks to one employee's idea, the brand we now link with Costco was born.

n152.text: Kirkland Signature, named for Kirkland, Costco's home base at the time.

n153.text: Costco picked certain product lines and began selling Kirkland-branded versions at 20% less than the supplier brands.

n156.text: Costco's secret to quality at low prices?

n157.text: Kirkland Signature products were made by top industry players.

n158.text: For example, Starbucks made Kirkland Signature coffee beans, Kimberly-Clark, known for Huggies, made the diapers, and Duracell made the batteries.

n159.text: So members got Starbucks-quality beans, Huggies-quality diapers and Duracell-quality batteries at low Kirkland Signature prices.

n160.text: It worked because tens of millions of Costco members

n161.text: were an opportunity no manufacturer could pass up.

n162.text: Costco took products from great brand makers,

n163.text: stripped the brand premium out of the price, and sold them under its own Kirkland Signature brand, so members got top-quality goods at low prices.

n164.text: As members came to see Kirkland Signature as both high-quality and affordable, sales kept growing and the brand's value rose too.

n165.text: Today, 550 of Costco's 4,000 products are Kirkland Signature, and the brand drives 25% of Costco's total sales. It's become a giant.

n166.text: In 2023, Kirkland Signature sales alone even topped the total revenue of Nike and Coca-Cola.

n167.text: Meanwhile, with strong member perks and cheap private labels, Costco took hold in the US and went global in the 1990s.

n168.text: In 1994, it teamed up with Shinsegae to open Korea's first membership warehouse store.

n169.text: But from 1998, it set up Costco Korea as its own company and began running the stores directly.

n171.text: foreign rivals like Walmart and Carrefour all pulled out. Only Costco survived, slowly growing around Seoul and other big cities.

n172.text: In 2017, co-founder Jim Sinegal said in an interview that Korea's Yangjae store topped sales among hundreds worldwide, thanking Koreans for loving Costco.

n173.text: As he suggested, Costco now rivals Korea's No. 2 hypermarket and keeps opening stores nationwide.

n174.text: E-Mart has answered with its own warehouse chain, Traders, but

n175.text: many observers say it'll be hard to stop Costco, the original membership warehouse.

n176.text: Let's keep an eye on how Costco's rivalry with E-Mart, Korea's top retailer, plays out.
